groups.title: Read an Academic Passage
groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
In many cities, traffic and machinery produce a constant, low-pitched roar. For birds, which rely on song to attract mates and defend their territory, this noise is a serious obstacle. A song that cannot be heard is of little use to the singer.

Researchers have found that several species adjust their behavior in response. Great tits living in noisy urban areas, for example, sing at a higher pitch than those in nearby forests, which allows their songs to rise above the rumble of engines. Other birds simply sing more loudly, and some, such as European robins, sing at night, when the streets are quieter. Because these changes can appear quickly, scientists believe that individual birds learn to modify their songs rather than inheriting new ones.

Such flexibility has limits, however. Singing louder requires more energy, and singing at night can reduce the time available for rest. Moreover, females of some species seem to prefer the lower-pitched songs that city noise drowns out, so males that adapt may be heard but judged less attractive. Species that cannot adjust at all tend to disappear from the noisiest neighborhoods. As a result, urban noise may gradually reduce the variety of birds that live alongside people.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
When shoppers choose between two products, their decision can be changed by adding a third option that almost no one wants. Marketers call this the decoy effect. The decoy is not really meant to be sold; its purpose is to make one of the other options look better by comparison.

A simple illustration involves drink sizes. Suppose a café sells a small coffee for $3 and a large one for $5. Many customers will choose the small. If the café adds a medium for $4.50, however, the large suddenly looks like a bargain, since it costs only slightly more than the medium. Sales of the large coffee typically rise, even though hardly anyone buys the medium. The customers' needs have not changed, yet their preferences have.

Psychologists explain the effect by noting that people rarely judge value in absolute terms. Because it is hard to know what a cup of coffee is truly worth, buyers look for easy comparisons, and the decoy supplies one. Critics argue that the practice manipulates consumers into spending more than they intended. Others reply that customers remain free to choose and that simply knowing about the technique is usually enough to resist it.

listening.script: Today I want to introduce the idea of a keystone species. That's an animal that has a much larger effect on its environment than you'd expect from its numbers. A classic example is the sea otter, which lives along the Pacific coast of North America. Sea otters eat a lot of sea urchins. Now, urchins are small, spiny animals that feed on kelp, a giant seaweed that grows in underwater forests. And these kelp forests are home to hundreds of kinds of fish and other animals. So what happens when the otters disappear? Well, we actually know, because in the eighteen hundreds, hunters killed most of them for their fur. Without otters, the number of urchins exploded. The urchins ate the kelp right down to the sea floor, and they left behind what scientists call urchin barrens, which are basically underwater deserts. The fish that depended on the kelp went away, too. Later, when otters were protected and returned to some areas, the kelp forests grew back, and so did the fish. In places where otters never returned, the barrens are still there. So the otter doesn't just live in the kelp forest. In a sense, it keeps the forest alive. Take it away, and the whole system changes.

options: How railroads were built across the United States

listening.script: Here's a question. When it's noon in one city, what time is it in a city three hundred kilometers to the west? Today, that's easy to answer. But in the early eighteen hundreds, it wasn't. Back then, every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun was highest in the sky. That meant noon in one town came a few minutes earlier or later than noon in the next town. And for most of history, nobody cared, because nobody could travel fast enough to notice. Then came the railroads. Suddenly, people could pass through several towns in a single hour, and every station kept its own local time. Imagine trying to read a train schedule! In the United States, railroad companies had to deal with dozens of different local times, and mistakes led to missed connections and even accidents. So, in eighteen eighty-three, the railroad companies agreed to divide the country into a small number of time zones. Inside each zone, every clock would show the same time. Some people complained that the railroads were changing the natural time, but the system was so practical that cities quickly adopted it. The following year, an international conference began extending the idea to the rest of the world.

listening.script: Let's say you have five hours to prepare for an exam. You could study for five hours the night before, or you could study one hour a day for five days. Same amount of time. Which is better? Well, more than a century of research gives a clear answer: spreading it out wins, and it isn't close. Psychologists call this the spacing effect. It was first described in the eighteen eighties by Hermann Ebbinghaus, who tested himself on lists of meaningless syllables, and it's been confirmed in hundreds of studies since. Why does it work? One explanation is that forgetting is actually useful. When you come back to material after a gap, you've forgotten some of it, so your brain has to work to rebuild the memory. That effort is what strengthens it. When you reread your notes five times in one night, by contrast, everything feels familiar, but that feeling is misleading. You're recognizing the material, not recalling it. And here's the irony. When students are asked which method works better, most choose cramming. It feels more productive, because the information is right there, fresh in your mind. Unfortunately, a week later, most of it is gone. So if you remember one thing from today, ideally after a short delay, it's this: study less at a time, but more often.

listening.script: When you picture an ancient Greek statue, you probably imagine smooth white marble. That image is so familiar that, for centuries, people assumed the Greeks wanted their statues white. They didn't. Most ancient statues were originally painted, often in bright blues, reds, and yellows, with detailed patterns on the clothing and even colored eyes and lips. So where did the color go? Well, paint is fragile. After two thousand years of sun, rain, and burial in the ground, most of it simply wore away. And here's an uncomfortable detail. When traces of paint did survive, some collectors in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries actually cleaned them off, because by then pure white marble had come to represent classical beauty. In other words, the ancient look we admire is partly a modern creation. How do we know what the originals looked like? Researchers shine ultraviolet light on the stone, which makes invisible traces of pigment glow. They also analyze tiny particles to identify the exact minerals that were used. From that evidence, they've built full-color reconstructions. Now, many visitors find these reconstructions, frankly, ugly. Too bright, almost like cartoons. But ask yourself whether that reaction tells us about the Greeks' taste or about our own. That's a question I'd like you to think about for next week.

groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Osei
professor.post: Over the next two weeks, we will look at how cities manage transportation. Some places, including the city of Tallinn in Estonia and the country of Luxembourg, have made buses and trams free for residents. Supporters say this reduces traffic and helps people with low incomes, while opponents worry about the cost. What do you think? Should cities make public transportation free for everyone? Why or why not?

students.name: Claire
students.post: I think free public transportation is a great idea. When people don't have to pay, more of them leave their cars at home, so there is less traffic and cleaner air. It also helps students and workers who spend a large part of their income just getting to school or to their jobs.

students.name: Andrew
students.post: I'm not sure that making transportation free solves the real problem. In my city, people avoid buses because they are slow and don't come often enough, not because of the price. I would rather see the money spent on more routes and more frequent service, even if riders still pay a small fare.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

In my opinion, cities should not make public transportation free for everyone, although I agree with Claire that cost matters for some riders. As Andrew points out, price is rarely the main reason people avoid buses. When a system loses its ticket income, it depends completely on tax money, and in difficult years the service may be cut, which hurts the very people it was meant to help. A fairer solution would be to keep normal fares but offer free passes to students, older people, and residents with low incomes. In this way, the people who truly need help receive it, while the city still has enough funds to add routes and run buses more often. A reliable system will attract far more drivers than a free one that is slow and crowded.

stages.instructions: Listen to the introduction. Then answer each of the interviewer's four questions after the beep. You have 45 seconds for each answer and no preparation time.

groups.title: Take an Interview
groups.instructions: You have agreed to take part in a research study about reading habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

toefl.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about reading habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: The last thing I read for pleasure was a novel that my sister gave me for my birthday. It is a detective story set in a small town by the sea, and I finished it in about three days because I could not stop reading. What I liked most was the main character, an older police officer who notices small details that everyone else misses. The ending also surprised me, because the person who committed the crime was someone I never suspected. After I finished it, I immediately looked for another book by the same author.

listening.script: Thank you for joining me today. To begin, please think about the last thing you read for pleasure, such as a book, a magazine, or an article online. What was it, and what did you like about it?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I usually prefer printed books, especially when I am reading for a long time. First, my eyes get tired when I look at a screen for more than an hour, and I already use a computer all day for my studies. Second, with a paper book I am not interrupted by messages or notifications, so I can concentrate better. However, I have to admit that reading on my phone is convenient when I am traveling, because I can carry many books without any extra weight. So I use both, but paper is still my first choice.

listening.script: People read in different ways. Some prefer printed books, while others would rather read on a phone or a tablet. Which do you usually prefer, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I only partly agree with that idea. It is probably true that young people read fewer novels and newspapers than their parents did, because there are so many other kinds of entertainment now, such as videos and games. On the other hand, I think young people actually read a great deal every day. They read messages, articles, and posts online for hours. The real change is that the texts are much shorter, so people have less practice concentrating on one long piece of writing. In my view, the problem is not the amount of reading but the type of reading.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people believe that young people today read less than earlier generations did. Do you agree? Why or why not?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: No, I don't think schools should set a fixed number of books for every student. When reading becomes a rule, many students treat it like a task to finish, and they may choose the shortest books just to reach the number. That does not make anyone love reading. I believe it is more effective to give students time to read during the school day and to let them choose books that match their interests. Teachers can still encourage them by recommending good titles and discussing them in class. If students enjoy what they read, they will naturally read more.

listening.script: Here is my last question. Do you think schools should require students to read a certain number of books every year? Why or why not?
